dgmm_2024_title: DGMM 2024 - Multi-Scale Component-Tree: A Hierarchical Representation for Sparse Objects
dgmm_2024_background_paragraph_1: The IAPR Third International Conference of Discrete Geometry and Mathematical Morphology (DGMM 2024) took place between the 15th and 19th April 2024 in Firenze (Florence), Italy. The official website of the conference can be consulted through this link.
dgmm_2024_background_paragraph_2: I gave a talk to support the publication of the article Multi-Scale Component-Tree: A Hierarchical Representation for Sparse Objects published in the conference proceedings (see this link). The main contribution of the MSCT is the addition of a new multi-scale decomposition (in spatial terms) in the structure of the component-tree. The newly-created tree is thus multi-scale in the spectral sense (as is the case for all component-trees) and in the spatial sense. The core idea is the keep as much as possible the pixel in non objects of interest (background) at low scale while iteratively enhancing the scale of objects of interest though successive partial component-tree computation. The MSCT if illustrated in the context of cell segmentation (and binary classification) on H&E Immunohistochemistry images.

dgmm_2024_general_principle_paragraph_1: The multi-scale component-tree (MSCT) is defined on a grayscale image by two-step construction process : one downsampling step and one upsampling step. The central idea is to build a complete representation of the input image (which means a component-tree) on a lower resolution of said image instead of the input image itself. This first step is illustrated by the top path (from left to right) on figure 2. The downsampling process is repeated multiple times, this number of repetitions being on the primary parameters guiding the construction of the MSCT. This operation is described in the step 1 section.
dgmm_2024_general_principle_paragraph_2: A component-tree is computed on the most downsampled image. It forms a complete representation of the input image but with a marginal computational cost. This structure forms the bases from which the MSCT will be built. From now on, this tree is labeled as the base component-tree. Its construction is described in the step 2 section. The second step of the construction process is more complex : it consists on applying a sort of reduced upsampling from the base component-tree and is applied as many times as the subsampling process was applied, the idea being that the selected areas will be augmented up to the resolution of the input image. The upsampling process corresponds to the lower path (from right to left) on figure 2.
dgmm_2024_general_principle_paragraph_3: The upsampling process is composed of multiple operations : an automatic selection of interesting nodes from the tree based on their content, the computation of partial sub-component-trees at a superior scale and the merging of these new sub-trees with the current tree at the local scale. The node selection process implies the definition of a metric used to measure the importance of each node in the tree. Once the representative nodes are identified, each sub-tree rooted on selected nodes will lead to the computation of a partial (local) component-tree at the superior scale. These two operations are described in the step 3 section. Finally, all computed sub-trees will have to be merged in replacement of the old sub-trees they represent at a finer scale. This non-trivial operation is described in the step 4 section.
dgmm_2024_downsampling_paragraph_1: In order to reduce the computation cost of the structure representing the image, we will use the most downsampled version of the input image. Keep in mind that this structure, the MSCT, has been theorised in the context of cell detection in histological images. In that specific context (although many other contexts apply), the images contain cell nuclei including some revealed by a reactive process (generally a chemical one) using one or multiple reactives. These nuclei which have reacted show a concentration of reactives which is translated by an elevated intensity at the location of the reaction and a low intensity in the absence of reaction.
dgmm_2024_downsampling_paragraph_2: To this effect, the chosen strategy must allow the conservation of the main features of the image, which means the maximal intensity peaks.An example is given in figure 3. The downsampling process applies a maximum filter on a 2 by 2 pixel sliding window. Technically speaking, it implies that the input image has to be a multiple of 2, an operation made prior to the described process.
dgmm_2024_base_component_tree_paragraph_: The base structure used to represent the image is built on the most downsampled image. The computational cost is minimal in regards to the original image and the areas of interest are preserved by the downsampling process. The structure in question is none other that a component-tree (or max-tree). It is a well known structure for which we have efficient algorithms for its computation. The base component-tree is the result of the computation of a component-tree on the most downsampled image.

The construction of component-tree (of max type) consists on applying successive thresholding of the image for each value in the value set (here from 0 to 255). For each threshold value, the obtained cut is binarized (pixels superior to the value are in white, pixels strictly inferior are in black) and the connected components are extracted. Each connected component produces a continuous shape of pixels oe each value (a flat zone), and is represented by a node in the tree. The relationship between the nodes encodes the spatial inclusion relation between the flat zones through the threshold values. An example of a component-tree computation is given in figure 4.
dgmm_2024_mser_paragraph_1: Now that we have a structure representing the image at low scale, we can enrich it by selecting interesting regions in the image (sub-trees in the tree) to refine. In order to do so, it is necessary to define a metric on the nodes of the tree. This metric should measure the importance of a node relative to the others. Ideally, nodes representing stable and well-defined flat zones, with a decent contrast to the background should be favourised with an elevated/low score in opposition to nodes representing unstable and/or low-contrasted flat zones. The metric choosen is based on the concept of MSER (maximally stable extremal regions).
dgmm_2024_mser_paragraph_2: The MSER algorithm outputs regions of the image which are both stable and distinct. The fact that these regions are stable and do not show significant differences when the image is the target of small perturbations is a major advantage. In fact, the node metric is quite noise resistant (like some blur) and only not affected too much by geometrical transformations (rotations). The distinctive character of output regions is important in itself because it signifies that the detected flat zones are sufficiently contrasted and correspond to the maximal intensity peaks.
dgmm_2024_mser_paragraph_3: The MSER computation consists of considering a parameter Δ which represents the difference of values in the value set of the image (here a gray level difference). The surface area of each connected component at level i is compared with the surface areas of the equivalent connected components at level i-Δ and i+Δ. The MSER value of a connected component is equal to |Qi+Δ∖Qi−Δ||Qi|. In a tree (MSCT or component-tree), this is equivalent to comparing the surface area (number of pixels) of the connected component at level λi-Δ (the sub-tree rooted in the red node in figure 5) minus the surface area of the connected components at level λi+Δ (the sub-trees rooted in the green nodes in figure 5) normalized by the surface area of the studied connected component (the sub-tree rooted in the blue node in figure 5) which is |Qλi−Δ∖Qλi+Δ||Qλi|. It is a simple metric to compute in such a tree. In addition, its calculus can be processes during the tree building.
dgmm_2024_mser_paragraph_4: From now on, we will need to select a set of nodes of interest to process from the MSCT. In order to do so, we propose the following node selection algorithm based on the MSER metric. A node priority queue is initialized and all nodes are placed inside by decreasing order of stability, that's to say by increasing order of MSER value. A set or result nodes is initialized empty. While the queue is not empty, the first node is poped and all ancestors and descendants of that node are gathered. The poped node is added to the result set. Finally, all ancestors and descendants of the node are removed from the priority queue. At the end, the set of result nodes contains the roots of sub-trees forming interesting flat zones according the their MSER stability. This algorithm garantees that all ouputed sub-trees are all mutually disjoint, which means that all branches contain sets of nodes that are all mutually disjoint. figure 6 gives an example of applying the described algorithm on the image of figure 4 which terminates in thee steps (images 2 to 4) and produces three areas of interest C, D and E.
dgmm_2024_pmt_paragraph_1: The MSCT is defined as being tied to a scale. The original image f0 is downsampled n times creating a set of downsampled images where fi is the image downsampled i−1 times from f0. The base component-tree is the component-tree of f0 that is Gn. The fully-enriched MSCT is the tree G0 having been subjected to n times the node selection process, the computation of partial component-trees and the merging of those with the current tree.
dgmm_2024_pmt_paragraph_2: The selection of nodes of interest has already been discussed in the previous section. Considering a MSCT Gi at a scale i. It contains nodes whose pixels are at most at the resolution of the image fi. The selected nodes in this tree corresponds to flat zones in the image fi. The idea is that for every sub-tree et so for every flat zone, a new hierarchy must be computed but at a finer scale. Said differently, we will compute a partial component-tree (only on the pixels of this flat zone) not on fi, but on fi−1. This implies to project the flat zone at this finer scale (a trivial operation) and to use it as a mask to compute a component-tree on fi−1. figure 7 gives an example of MSCT Gi with the associated image fi and the selected sub-tree in red. figure 8 shows the image fi−1 with the flat zone projected in red and the resulting partial component-tree. It is important to note that, in order to complete one step of the upsampling process, all the resulting partial component-trees must now be merged with Gi in order to produce the MSCT Gi−1.
dgmm_2024_pmt_paragraph_3: The merging of partial component-trees is not a trivial operation. With the given downsampling process, a large number of values of the image are lost between f0 and fn. However, ant since we compute the partial component-trees in an image at a finer scale, a subset of those values are nontheless reintroduced. It is the case presented in figure 9 where the merged tree (right) contains nodes whose values does not exist in its downsampled version (left). In addition, when increasing the scale, new connected components which, at a lower scale only form a single connected component, can form distinct connected components creating on this occasion new branches on nodes which have not been selected for treatment. It is the case shown in figure 10. That said, it is important to mention a property of the merging operation (also called tree enrichment), that the order of fusion does not matter. In fact, the partial component-trees can be merged in any order with the MSCT. This property is the notable consequence of the proposed node selection algorithm (via the MSER metric of the nodes) which ouputs a set of sub-trees all mutually disjoint.
